title: The hidden Christians of Japan
hook: after the Nagasaki martyrs, families kept the faith in secret, with no priests, for generations

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vietnamese martyrs, full of joy, and not alone: priests, catechists and families who held on under persecution. Did one of their names stay with you? Today, another coast, and a faith that went underground. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

A small white figure of a woman holding a child sits on a farmhouse shelf in Japan. To a visiting official it looks like Kannon, a Buddhist figure of mercy. To the family who owns it, it is also Maria. Christianity has been banned. Missionaries have been sent away, and on a hill at Nagasaki, Paul Miki and his companions were crucified for the faith. After that, in fishing villages and on small islands, families went on praying anyway. Quietly. With no priests at all. Children grew up, had children, and passed it on. Today: the hidden Christians of Japan.
screen: `A MOTHER AND CHILD ON A SHELF.` → `THE FAITH IS BANNED.` → `NO PRIESTS AT ALL.`

segments.voice: Japanese has a name for them: kakure kirishitan, hidden Christians. Some historians keep that name for the groups who stayed apart after the ban was lifted, and call the families of the hidden years senpuku, underground. First, the hiding. The faith lived inside ordinary households: a figure on a shelf that could pass for something else, prayers said quietly at home, feasts kept without anyone outside noticing. Second, the laypeople. With no priests, there was no Mass and no confession. But the Church teaches that in need, anyone with the right intention can baptize. So villages chose baptizers, and the water and the words kept going. They kept a calendar of feasts, and prayers handed down by heart, called orasho. Third, the memory. With no books out in the open, prayers were learned by ear. Over the generations some words wore smooth, like stones in a river, a mix of Latin, Portuguese and Japanese sounds. Fourth, the return. When missionaries came back and built a church in Nagasaki, tradition says a group of villagers came to the French priest there, Bernard Petitjean, and a woman whispered that their hearts were the same as his. Then they asked him where the statue of Santa Maria was. Not every hidden community joined the Church again after that; some kept the ways they had guarded so long. In the Gospel of Luke, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his disciples: "Fear not, little flock." A little flock, kept for generations by nothing but memory.
screen: `A FAITH BEHIND A SHELF.` · `LAY BAPTIZERS, PRAYERS BY HEART.` · `WORDS WORN SMOOTH BY MEMORY.` · `OUR HEARTS ARE THE SAME AS YOURS.` · then, large: `FEAR NOT, LITTLE FLOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a small faithful habit. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you could do every day that holds what matters to you. A line said on waking. A sign of the cross. A minute of quiet before the phone. A thank-you before eating. Something so small nobody else would notice. If you pray, you can say a prayer you know by heart, slowly, the way those families kept theirs. If you don't, hold the habit in mind and see where it fits tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Kakure kirishitan. Japanese for hidden Christians, families who kept baptism, feasts and prayers alive in secret, without priests, generation after generation.
Your line: 250 years in secret. Today, do your small faithful habit once, where no one sees it, and keep it the way a family keeps something worth handing on. Day eight hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Catholics in Japan keep the feast of Paul Miki and his companions, and pilgrims visit the churches and villages around Nagasaki linked to the hidden Christians.

trapdoor: what you thought: a few people hid their faith for a while.
what it means: generation after generation with no priests, baptizing their own children and praying by heart.
what a scholar hears: orasho, prayers learned by ear until the words wore smooth, and communities that did not all rejoin the Church when missionaries returned.

notes: Claims rule: the index carry '250 years in secret' is kept exactly as required, but no cited text for the day states the figure; the spoken script otherwise avoids dates and counts ('generation after generation'). The index hook's '1597' and '250 years' were left out of the hook field. Owner/Keeper may want to soften the carry in the outline.
Fumie (stepping on images) and the tradition that some stepped and then sought forgiveness (e.g., contrition prayers among the hidden communities): confirm phrasing.
Maria Kannon figures described as looking like Kannon to officials and being Maria to the family: confirm; framed neutrally, no comparison of traditions intended.
Orasho as the name for the prayers, and the description of words drifting in sound: confirm. The common derivation from Latin oratio was deliberately not stated in the spoken script.
The 'discovery' at Oura church (woman whispering that their hearts were the same; asking for Santa Maria's statue) is attributed to tradition; confirm against Petitjean's letters.
Some communities (kakure kirishitan in the narrow sense) did not rejoin the Church: confirm wording is fair.
Japanese script 隠れキリシタン and pronunciation: confirm.
